notes.title: Model exact quantities with decimal or integral representations
notes.core: Treat binary floating point as approximate; for ledger amounts and decimal policies use integer minor units with checked bounds or decimal arithmetic with explicit input and rounding contracts.
rules: Represent integral minor units with long when supported by currency scale and safe arithmetic ranges; validate the currency and fraction scale at boundaries.
Use BigDecimal(String) or BigDecimal.valueOf(double) intentionally; avoid BigDecimal(double) when intending the human decimal spelling of a binary float.
Prefer compareTo for numeric decimal order; equals considers the representation scale, so 1.0 and 1.00 may compare equal but not be equal objects.
Never silently round a decimal division: specify scale and RoundingMode when a nonterminating quotient is possible.
Use Math.addExact, Math.multiplyExact or dedicated checked-bound routines when fixed-width integer overflow must fail rather than wrap.
Do not assume floating-point arithmetic becomes exact by rounding only the printed output; the errors can affect branching and cumulative decisions.
nuance: Not all domains need exact decimal results: approximate scientific measurements and statistical models often appropriately use double.
BigDecimal remains sensitive to origin and scale; valueOf(double) first reflects Double.toString, not the original real number or decimal user intent.
Different currencies may require differing legal minor units, rounding rules and settlement boundaries, and integer cents cannot encode every asset.
Division without an explicit MathContext or terminating expansion may throw ArithmeticException rather than return an approximate answer.
Microbenchmark claims about decimal versus integer performance should be tested against the deployed JDK and business constraints.
notes.misconception: Double is safe for a ledger if the UI rounds to two digits at the end.
notes.production_context: A multi-currency billing pipeline carries typed CurrencyCode and long scaled amounts for supported currencies, using BigDecimal and an explicit rounding policy for calculated fees.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 preserves BigDecimal scale, compareTo, valueOf, and Math exact arithmetic APIs; benchmark modern JDK behavior before choosing a performance-sensitive representation.

notes.title: Choose primitive and boxed numeric values by contract
notes.core: Prefer primitive types for ordinary numeric computation; use wrappers deliberately only when nullability, generics or reference semantics require them, avoiding identity comparisons and implicit unboxing hazards.
rules: Use int/long/double/boolean instead of wrappers when absence is not part of the API and collection/generic storage is not required.
Compare wrapper contents with equals, primitive comparison methods or an explicit unboxed value; avoid == to test numeric equality of distinct wrapper references.
Document whether a boxed parameter can be null; null unboxing can throw NullPointerException even when the eventual expression looks numeric.
Choose Comparator.comparingInt or Integer.compare for integer comparator contracts; do not subtract arbitrary ints because subtraction can overflow.
Use primitive operators and streams when allocation profiling justifies it; avoid repeatedly boxing and unboxing inside hot loops.
Keep wrapper null as a distinct domain state where needed; reject, default, or represent optional absence explicitly before computing.
nuance: Wrapper caches are implementation/version details unsuitable as a numeric-equality rule; a passing == comparison within a small range proves nothing.
Autounboxing can happen inside ternary expressions and arithmetic mixed with wrappers, which may hide a null failure.
Java generics do not accept primitive type arguments (List<int>), so wrapper types remain necessary in ordinary generic collections.
A primitive OptionalInt can describe an optional primitive result without encoding absence as a boxed null.
Java21 value-oriented wrapper guidance does not give identity stability; never synchronize on wrappers or require unique wrapper identities.
notes.misconception: Autoboxing makes Integer and int interchangeable, including null and object identity.
notes.production_context: A transaction counter uses primitive long state and Long.compare for ordering; an optional imported numeric field is validated before conversion to primitive counters.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 continues boxing/unboxing and wrapper caching behavior with warnings against identity-sensitive use of value-based wrapper objects; prefer primitive specializations on hot paths.

notes.title: Represent domain values and capabilities with actual types
notes.core: Use strings for text and boundary serialization, not as unchecked stand-ins for money, state, structured aggregates or keys granting access to a capability.
rules: Parse external strings once into validated domain types: enums, numeric values, immutable records or identifiers, and reject unknown values deliberately.
Do not concatenate fields with homemade separators to represent an aggregate; delimiters may occur in data and parsing contracts can drift.
Use typed opaque references for capabilities or per-context storage; a user-selected string key should not authorize access to an unrelated namespace.
Represent operational status with a closed enum or sealed domain result when appropriate, not unvalidated magic string protocols throughout core code.
Use a record or class with clear equals/hashCode and defensive policies for composite keys rather than fragile string concatenation.
Keep interoperation and log strings at explicit boundaries, avoiding unvalidated raw strings that leak into domain API internals.
nuance: Protocol and persistence formats are often legitimately string-valued; not every string should be replaced by a custom type.
A record is a concise value aggregate in Java21 but will not automatically validate security/currency/id constraints.
ThreadLocal provides typed storage by reference identity per thread, but thread pools demand remove or scoped lifecycle to avoid retaining stale values.
A typed key prevents accidental collisions, not malicious authorization bypass by itself; enforce access checks at the trust boundary.
Enum.name() and toString() are not universal stable wire contracts; use explicit codes when external compatibility matters.
notes.misconception: A separator-delimited String is as robust as a record and a string token is a secure capability.
notes.production_context: An audit trail uses a validated AuditKey record and typed status enum; request context uses a private ThreadLocal key cleaned up after each pooled worker operation.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 records and sealed types make typed aggregates and state models concise; ThreadLocal remains usable but virtual-thread/context-lifecycle decisions require separate review.

notes.title: Accumulate long strings without repeated immutable copying
notes.core: A short fixed expression with + remains readable; for loops accumulating a potentially large number of fragments, append into a StringBuilder, stream or writer instead of repeatedly constructing intermediate strings.
rules: Use a local StringBuilder when building a potentially long dynamically sized result over repeated iterations.
Allow straightforward + for small bounded concatenations; Java compilers optimize many single-expression concatenations.
Preserve ordering, separators and null policies when replacing a concatenation loop with an accumulator.
For huge outputs consider streaming to an Appendable, BufferedWriter or another consumer rather than materializing all data in memory.
Optionally pre-size a builder using safe, measured size estimates and check integer overflow for massive constructions.
Benchmark realistic repeated-concatenation workloads on Java 21 rather than repeating old fixed speedup ratios.
nuance: StringBuilder is mutable and generally not suitable as a shared unsynchronized mutable buffer; keep its lifetime local.
Java21 uses modern invokedynamic string concatenation strategies for many expressions, but does not guarantee that x += fragment inside a loop avoids repeated copying.
String.join or Collectors.joining may be appropriate with clear separator rules, though they too materialize output.
Do not prematurely allocate extremely large buffers from unchecked item count times estimated width.
For short output, clarity often outweighs allocation differences; do not claim a particular asymptotic cost for every optimizer implementation without measurement.
notes.misconception: Modern string concatenation optimization makes repeated + inside loops equivalent to a single builder across all workloads.
notes.production_context: A billing export streams rows to a Writer; small status labels use + while medium-sized audit summaries use a local StringBuilder with explicit delimiters.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 string concatenation internals have evolved since the Java 9-era publication; validate performance empirically but preserve the immutable-copying design concern.

notes.title: Code to interface contracts without losing semantics
notes.core: Declare clients, variables and return types with the most appropriate interface or abstract contract so implementations can vary, while preserving all requirements not expressed by the interface alone.
rules: Use Set, Map, List, Collection or domain interfaces when clients need only their documented operations rather than one concrete class.
Preserve observable ordering, null handling, mutability and concurrency semantics when substituting implementations—even if interfaces compile unchanged.
Use concrete classes when no meaningful interface exists, particularly immutable value types and certain framework contracts.
Select the least specific type that actually supports the required behavior; use a base class where a class-based framework has no usable interface.
Avoid leaking HashMap, ArrayList or other concrete collection types through fields and method signatures without domain justification.
Test substitution using boundary behavior: predictable order, duplicate suppression, permitted nulls and output ownership.
nuance: Set does not promise iteration order: LinkedHashSet and TreeSet carry additional semantics that a plain HashSet replacement may violate.
Java21 SequencedSet offers explicit first/last and order-related operations; it does not mean any Set can truthfully be treated as sequenced.
Map.of and List.of are unmodifiable and reject nulls; they are not behaviorally equivalent to arbitrary mutable concrete implementations.
An EnumMap needs enum keys; selecting it may improve certain behaviors but cannot substitute for all Map types.
A domain-specific interface should not exist solely to conceal simple immutable value objects such as String or BigInteger.
notes.misconception: If both implementations satisfy the same interface, changing them cannot affect program behavior.
notes.production_context: A routing table exposes Map<Region,Policy> and relies on explicit ordered iteration only where a SequencedMap or ordered domain contract is promised, never on unspecified HashMap traversal.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 adds SequencedCollection, SequencedSet and SequencedMap, which help express ordered contracts when they are actually required.
